solution:
The stem is the standard definition of **sustainable development**. Section 16.2 of this chapter states it in almost the same words: "Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present, without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own need."

The other three alternatives are not defined anywhere in the chapter and none of them carries this meaning. "Continuous development" and "true development" say nothing about future generations at all, and "irrational development" is the opposite of a development that conserves resources for the future. Only the second alternative names the concept the stem describes, so the correct option is sustainable development.

[Textbook misprint: the stem is printed with a Greek capital upsilon, \(\Upsilon\), where a lower-case gamma, \(\gamma\), belongs - the question is about the \(\gamma\)-isomer of BHC. The glyph is transcribed exactly as printed. The chapter itself makes the intention plain: section 16.3, principle 3, prints the same wrong glyph and then glosses it, "One of the \(\Upsilon\)-isomer (gamma) of BHC is called gammexane or lindane". The answer is unaffected.]

BHC is benzene hexachloride, \(\mathrm{C_6H_6Cl_6}\). It exists in several stereoisomers, and the chapter names the one that is insecticidal. In principle 3 (Less hazardous chemical synthesis) it states: "Nowadays benzene hexachloride (BHC) is used as insecticide. One of the \(\Upsilon\)-isomer (gamma) of BHC is called gammexane or lindane."

Testing the other three: DDT is dichlorodiphenyl trichloroethane, a different compound entirely, and the same paragraph names it as the *earlier* insecticide that BHC replaced. Chloroform is \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) and chlorobenzene is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl}\); neither has the molecular formula of BHC, so neither can be an isomer of it. Lindane is therefore the only alternative that is an isomer of BHC at all.

Section 16.5 (c. Why Nano ?) states the origin of the prefix directly: "'Nano' in Greek means dwarf but in actual case 'nano' is even smaller than dwarf."

So the language is **Greek** and the meaning is **dwarf**, which rules out the three alternatives on two independent counts each: they name the wrong language (French, Spanish, Latin) and the wrong meaning (billion, particle, invisible). The "billion" alternative is the near-miss worth naming, because one nanometre really is one billionth of a metre \(\left(1\ \mathrm{nm} = 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\right)\) — but that is what the prefix *denotes*, not what the Greek word *means*, and the language given with it is wrong in any case.

Table 16.1 of section 16.7.3 lists each characterization technique against the information it yields. Against FTIR (Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy) it records "Absorption by functional groups, Binding nature." An infrared spectrum is a record of the frequencies a sample absorbs, and each absorption band belongs to a particular functional group, so FTIR identifies the functional groups present.

The same table assigns each of the other three alternatives to a different technique: "particle size" to XRD and TEM, "preliminary confirmation of formation of nanoparticles" to UV-visible spectroscopy, and "crystal structure" to XRD. None of them is listed against FTIR, so absorption of functional groups is the only alternative the table supports.

Section 16.1 states it outright: "The concept of green chemistry was coined by Paul T. Anastas." The "Do you know ?" box on the same page adds that he directs Yale University's Center for Green Chemistry and Green Engineering and is known as the father of green chemistry, and section 16.1 also credits him with enunciating the twelve principles of green chemistry.

The chapter itself falsifies two of the other three alternatives. It records that "the term 'nanotechnology' was defined by Tokyo Science University Professor, Nario Taniguchi in 1974", and Fig. 16.13 places Richard Feynman in 1959 among the scientists who contributed to nanotechnology — both belong to nanotechnology, not green chemistry. "Born Haber" is not a person at all but the Born-Haber cycle, a thermochemical cycle for lattice enthalpy, and it appears nowhere in this chapter. Paul T. Anastas is therefore the only alternative connected with green chemistry.
